newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek cabinet meets to deal with defiant farmers.
newsitem.headline: Greek cabinet meets to deal with defiant farmers.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis came under growing pressure on Tuesday to take action to end a blockade by angry farmers that has paralysed the national road and rail network for nearly two weeks.
"Make a move Mr Prime Minister," Eleftherotypia newspaper said in an open letter to Simitis as the cabinet held a meeting expected to be dominated by the crisis.
"The country is paralysed, the economy has huge problems and industry and export companies have suffered immense damages," the paper said, adding: "This situation can't go on any longer."

Doctors, teachers, public servants and customs workers have joined in protests against Simitis's tight 1997 budget with marches through Athens and rallies outside parliament, where the cabinet is meeting. But the farmers are Simitis's biggest problem.

The government has tried to play down the cabinet meeting, saying it was routine and would deal with civil servants' wages. But political commentators said it would be dominated by the search for a solution to the farmers' dispute.

So far the government has chosen to face down the farmers in the hope that they would eventually run out of steam. Instead the barricades of tractors have grown by the day, blocking most roads in central, northern and southern Greece.

"We can stay here until March when the next farming season starts. We don't have the money to move the tractors anyway," said Dimitris Kelesides, an onion grower from central Larissa, headquarters of the farmers' protest.
Farmers, pressing for cheaper fuel and state subsidies for their products, have blocked nearly 100 points around Greece, causing chaos for domestic and international transport.

Hundreds of trucks from Europe, the Balkans and the Middle East are trapped in Greece. Drivers are having to stay with their vehicles, despite lack of food and sanitation, for fear of their cargoes being stolen.
Borders with Bulgaria and Turkey have been closed and Athens has been cut off by land from Greece's second city of Salonika in the north.

"Nothing is moving," said Anastasis Kostopoulos, who owns a gas station on the Athens-Salonika highway outside Larissa. "I used to sell about 1,500 litres (330 gallons) of fuel a day and now I sell less than 90 (20 gallons). I'm being ruined."
On the Bulgarian side of the border the blockade has caused a two-km (1.2-mile) traffic jam. Trucks have been stranded with no food and tonnes of perishable products like milk and meat.

"I feel like a hostage," said British trucker Alan Kendall, who is stranded at a roadblock north of Larissa. "I also want cheaper diesel but I don't go out blocking national roads. This is a Greek thing anyway and I should not have to pay for it."
Simitis and his ministers have told the farmers there is no money to satisfy their demands and warned them the government will not give in to blackmail.

Simitis is facing his first major test since winning elections in September. His tight 1997 budget, intended to prepare Greece for the EU single currency, has caused a wave of protest by various groups asked to pay more taxes next year.
